conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s just 10 gentle questions about the past week, and everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is at risk. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause any moment. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, I do laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes a silly face or when the baby does something cute—but it feels like I have to work harder to find that lighter side. Most days it’s just kind of “meh,” and the giggles don’t come as naturally as they used to before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes—maybe not every day, but here and there. Like yesterday my partner tripped over the diaper bag and we both cracked up for a second. It felt nice, but I notice those moments are kind of brief and I go right back to feeling tired and worried.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when I think about taking the baby for a walk if the weather’s nice—but it’s not the same steady “can’t-wait” feeling I used to have. Most plans feel more like chores I have to push myself through rather than things I truly look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I’m just not soothing her right. Deep down I know babies just cry, but the “what-if-it’s-my-fault” thought still sneaks in a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she feels warm, or I’ll lie down and obsess that the crib mattress isn’t firm enough—even though I triple-checked it. Nothing big has actually gone wrong, but my mind keeps jumping to the worst-case scenario anyway.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky, but there are moments—especially at night—when I’ll suddenly feel this rush of dread, like something bad is about to happen. My chest gets tight and I have to remind myself to breathe. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling because there’s no real reason for it.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days I feel like I’m juggling more balls than I have hands for. I’ll start a load of laundry, the baby cries, I have to heat a bottle, remember I still haven’t eaten, and suddenly I’m standing in the kitchen on the verge of tears because it all feels like too much. I manage, but it’s like I’m constantly one step behind myself.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not so much that I’m lying there sobbing—just this low-level unhappiness that keeps churning. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed, and then my brain starts replaying every little thing I think I did wrong that day. I drift off eventually, but I wake up a lot and never feel really rested.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel sad some of the time—like a gray cloud that comes and goes. I’ll be fine for a couple of hours, especially if the baby smiles or I get a nice text from a friend, but then the heaviness settles back in. It’s not every moment, but it’s definitely there more days than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not every day—maybe two or three times this past week. It’s usually when I’m extra tired and the baby won’t settle; I’ll just feel this wave of “I can’t do this” and the tears slip out. They don’t last long, but it surprises me because I’m not normally a crier.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. I’ve never had any thoughts like that. I just want to feel like myself again so I can take care of my baby the way I know I’m supposed to.

You've shared that the joy of new motherhood has been clouded by daily <sym>worry</sym>, frequent <sym>sadness</sym>, and moments of <sym>panic</sym> that leave you feeling constantly one step behind. Although you can still laugh or look forward to small outings, these bright spots are brief, and most tasks now feel like chores. You described crying a few times this week when exhaustion peaks, and nights are restless even after the baby settles, yet you remain motivated to feel like yourself again and are keeping both your baby and yourself safe.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient can occasionally laugh, but describes the moments as brief and immediately overshadowed by fatigue and worry, aligning with "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only sporadic enjoyment and a clear reduction in anticipatory pleasure, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming thoughts "a few times a week" and gives concrete examples, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, worst-case-scenario worries without real triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of intense dread and physical anxiety symptoms without cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and juggling struggles, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sleep disruption due to rumination and low mood, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent sadness that "comes and goes" and is present "more days than not," aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 18 meets the ≥14 threshold for <med>probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Key items scoring 2-3 describe near-daily <sym>generalized anxiety</sym> and <sym>episodic panic</sym>, persistent <sym>low mood</sym> with crying, <sym>self-reproach</sym>, and marked <sym>reduced enjoyment</sym>. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for <med>Major Depressive Disorder</med>: ≥5 symptoms, same 2-week period, causing clinically significant distress or impairment, with onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum. No self-harm ideation keeps acute safety risk lower, but functional impairment warrants prompt evaluation and treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Discuss evidence-based options including <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Encourage 20-30 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of help with household tasks to reduce overwhelm
4. Provide resources: Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773, local mother-and-baby unit contacts
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (partner present) – infant approx. 2–6 wks old  
Instrument: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) – clinician-guided interview  
Date: ____________

1. Positive Screening Items (clinically elevated):
   - Anhedonia / reduced pleasure (Q2) – “little sparks” but plans feel like chores  
   - Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3) – attributes infant fussiness to own actions  
   - Generalized anxiety & nocturnal panic (Q4, Q5) – daily worry, episodic chest tightness  
   - Subjective overwhelm / coping deficit (Q6) – “juggling more balls than hands”  
   - Sleep disruption secondary to mood rumination (Q7) – difficulty falling/staying asleep  
   - Persistent low mood & crying spells (Q8, Q9) – “gray cloud” several days/wk  
   - Functional impact – daily tasks impaired; never feels rested  

2. Endorsements at Level 1–2 (mild–moderate):
   - Laughing ability (Q1) – present but fleeting  
   - Panic intensity (Q5) – distressing surges, not full attacks  

3. Protective / Negative Findings:
   - NO self-harm ideation (Q10) – explicitly denied  
   - Maintains attachment to infant & partner – motivated to “feel like myself again”

4. Risk Pattern:
   Meets screening threshold for probable **postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features**; impairment consistent across mood, anxiety, and coping domains. No acute safety concerns identified today.

5. Next Steps (screening level):
   - Review EPDS numerical score; if ≥10 proceed to full assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, psychosocial intake)  
   - Provide psycho-education, normalize help-seeking, offer referral to OB mental-health team or perinatal psychiatry  
   - Schedule follow-up within 1–2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and safety

Clinician: ____________  
Signature: ____________
